### [CHUNK FLEX-02] Objectives, hypothesis, approach | source: S1 | tags: objectives, hypothesis, approach
- Objectives [SRC]: (1) map flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity; (2) measure effectiveness of gaseous suppressants (CO2, He, SF6); (3) build predictive models of combustion limits in reduced gravity, validating simplified models by adding detailed chemistry, heat transfer and transport; (4) obtain high-resolution droplet burning rate, extinction, radiation, soot and temperature data across ambient conditions and suppressant levels.
- Hypothesis [SRC]: absence of buoyant convection changes species/energy transport, radiative loss and kinetics, so flammability limits and suppressant efficacy differ from normal gravity.
- Approach [SRC]: ignite relatively large droplets and determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure (0.5-1.5 atm), then repeat with suppressants. Includes slow, sub-buoyant flow tests made by translating the droplet at a slow uniform speed, and many free (fiber-free) droplets with slow drift.
- Claimed Earth benefits [SRC]: fire safety in confined or reduced-gravity settings (submarines, high-altitude aircraft); less harmful suppressants; cool-flame chemistry informing engines with better efficiency and lower emissions.
- [INF] The PSI text names "He, CO2, SF6" while the 2013 slides (S3) say N2, He, CO2 and xenon were flown. See FLEX-14.

### [CHUNK FLEX-03] Core concepts and equations (LaTeX) | source: S4, S5, S7, S6 | tags: equations, theory, glossary
1. Classical d-square law (no soot, no radiation, quasi-steady) [SRC, S4]:
   $$\left(\frac{D}{D_0}\right)^2 = 1 - K_0\,\frac{t}{D_0^2}, \qquad \text{equivalently } D^2 = D_0^2 - K t$$
   Real droplets deviate. K depends on $D_0$ (S4, FLEX-09).
2. Standoff ratios [SRC, S4]: flame standoff ratio $\mathrm{FSR}=D_f/D$, soot-shell standoff ratio $\mathrm{SSR}=D_s/D$.
3. Limiting Oxygen Index and Minimum Extinction Concentration [SRC, S7]:
   $$\mathrm{LOI} = 0.209\,(1-\mathrm{MEC})$$
   LOI is the lowest O2 mole fraction that supports a quasi-steady flame. For total flooding, the agent must drop O2 below LOI. [SRC]
4. Damkohler framing [SRC S7, definition added] The flammability boundary is essentially the critical Damkohler number, $\mathrm{Da}=\tau_{\text{residence}}/\tau_{\text{chemistry}}$. Below the critical value the flame cannot be sustained. The exact definition is not given in the source. [INF]
5. Two classical extinction modes [SRC, S3, S7]: diffusive/blowoff extinction (high O2, small droplet; red branch, Law 1975) and radiative extinction (low O2, large droplet; blue branch, Chao et al. 1990). After extinction the droplet continues as pure evaporation.
6. Generic overall-reaction form used in activation-energy analyses [INF]:
   $$\dot{\omega} = B\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)[\text{Fuel}]^{a}[\text{O}_2]^{b}$$
   Nayagam et al. extracted an effective heat release, overall activation energy and pre-exponential factor from burning rates and extinction diameters. The numeric values are not in the supplied text. [FLAG]
7. Methanol two-step global kinetics (Zhang 1996, in S6) [SRC]:
   $$2\,\mathrm{CH_3OH}+\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow \mathrm{H_2O}+\mathrm{CO_2}+3\,\mathrm{H_2}+\mathrm{CO}, \qquad \mathrm{H_2}+\mathrm{CO}+\mathrm{O_2}\rightarrow \mathrm{H_2O}+\mathrm{CO_2}$$
   Reaction II is written schematically in the slide. It is not stoichiometrically scaled to the H2 produced in reaction I.
8. Methanol extinction-diameter theory (Zhang, Card, Williams 1996, via S6) [SRC]: extinction diameter $d_e$ is linear in initial diameter, $d_e \propto d_0$. Water produced in the flame diffuses back and condenses on the droplet, builds up in the second half of burning, and at a threshold begins to evaporate with the fuel. That water reaches the flame zone, lowers flame temperature, raises reaction time, and the flame extinguishes when residence time is insufficient.
9. Simulation governing equations (S5) [SRC, summarized]: 1-D spherosymmetric transient species and energy conservation in both phases; heat flux = conduction + enthalpy transport by species diffusion + Dufour effect + spectral radiation; Stefan-Maxwell diffusion; far field at 200 x initial droplet diameter, fixed composition and 298 K. Interface equilibrium (reconstructed from garbled text) [INF]: $x_{i,\text{gas}}\,p=\gamma_i\,x_{i,\text{liq}}\,p_{\text{vap},i}(T)$.

### [CHUNK FLEX-04] LOI test procedure | source: S1, S7 | tags: procedure, LOI, flammability-map
Construct the flammability map (O2 mole fraction vs droplet diameter) as follows [SRC]:
1. Select test pressure 0.5-1.5 atm.
2. Select a smaller droplet (about 3 mm).
3. Choose an O2 fraction, based on ground tests, that lets the droplet burn to completion.
4. Run a droplet combustion test.
5. If the flame extinguishes at a finite diameter, enlarge the droplet or repeat.
6. Continue until the flame survives only briefly after ignition (radiative extinction).
7. Repeat at lower O2 fraction.
8. Continue to the O2 fraction where the droplet does not ignite.
If extinction sizes are too small to measure at every O2 level, run an iterative sequence (burn to completion, then no-ignition) with finer O2 increments to bracket LOI. [SRC]
Slow-flow tests: duplicate runs that gave finite extinction diameters, then near the end impose a small sub-buoyant flow by translating the droplet. Hardware could not diagnose a uniform steady convective flow over a whole test. [SRC]
Suppressant tests repeat the same procedure at fixed suppressant level, then step the level and type. [SRC]
Conceptual map (S7 Fig. 2): flammable region inside a U-shaped curve; red branch = extinction (blowoff), blue branch = radiative quench; LOI = point where they meet (lowest O2 supporting a quasi-steady flame). [SRC]

### [CHUNK FLEX-05] Suppressant efficacy: MEC, LOI, CO2 vs He | source: S7 | tags: suppression, CO2, helium, MEC, LOI, calc
- ISS US segment uses CO2 as suppressant. [SRC]
- Cup-burner methane flames, standard air (Takahashi et al. 2004), MEC [SRC]:
  CO2: 0.16 (1-g), 0.19 (micro-g). He: 0.27 (1-g), 0.31 (micro-g). N2: 0.26 (1-g), 0.38 (micro-g).
- LOI from $\mathrm{LOI}=0.209(1-\mathrm{MEC})$ [CALC]:
  | Agent | LOI 1-g | LOI micro-g | change |
  | CO2 | 0.176 | 0.169 | -0.007 |
  | He  | 0.153 | 0.144 | -0.008 |
  | N2  | 0.155 | 0.130 | -0.025 |
  (rounded to 3 decimals)
- Reading [INF]: lower MEC means a more effective agent. By cup-burner MEC, CO2 is the most effective of the three in both gravity levels. N2 loses the most effectiveness in micro-g (MEC rises 0.26 to 0.38).
- Conflicting evidence [SRC]: Honda and Ronney 1998 (opposed-flow flame spread over thin solids with He, N2, Ar, CO2, SF6) suggest CO2 is less effective than He in microgravity on a minimum-O2 basis. The two results differ in fuel and geometry, so no single ranking holds. [INF]
- Katta et al. 2004 (methane cup burner, simulation plus micro-g experiment): CO2 above 19.1 vol% needed to destabilize the flame base in micro-g, vs 16.4 vol% in normal gravity. Gas-phase radiation is important for micro-g limits. [SRC]
- Radiative feedback: with no buoyant convection, flame radiative losses become a large share of heat loss; a thermally participating gas like CO2 absorbs and re-radiates, raising fuel-side temperatures (Chernovsky et al. 2005, ethylene flame on a spherical porous burner, 20-40% CO2). This is why CO2 efficacy in micro-g is not assured. [SRC]

- Diagnostics requirements (S7 section 5.2) [SRC]: chamber gas temperature accuracy at least +/-0.5 C and pressure at least +/-0.01 atm, sampled at 10 Hz or faster; all data time-synchronized to GMT within +/-0.03 s.
- Machine use: this is a ready-made design-of-experiments grid. An agent can rebuild it from the table above, or load the original Tables 6-12 from the PDF.

>>> source: RAG/Tamer.txt | chunk: FLEX-07 | location: lines 100-110 | mapping: FLEX deep analysis pack (file header: FLEX, PSI-69); header names no other experiment
### [CHUNK FLEX-07] Cool-flame discovery (n-heptane) | source: S3, S4-ref, S5 | tags: cool-flame, discovery, heptane, fire-safety
- Conventional view before FLEX [SRC, S3]: a droplet flame extinguishes by diffusive extinction (high O2, small droplet) or radiative extinction (low O2, large droplet), followed by pure evaporation. Cool flames were traditionally tied to premixed combustion and engine knock (cool flame leads to hot ignition).
- Anomaly [SRC]: after radiative extinction of a large n-heptane droplet (the visible flame disappears), the droplet keeps regressing at a quasi-steady burning rate for an extended period, ends at a finite "cool-flame extinction" diameter, and then a vapor cloud rapidly appears around the droplet. [SRC, Nayagam et al. 2012 abstract on S3 slide]
- Hypothesis: the second stage is sustained by low-temperature, soot-free "cool-flame" chemical heat release. Measured burning rates and extinction diameters give effective activation energy and pre-exponential values closer to literature cool-flame values than hot-flame values. [SRC]
- Never before seen in 50+ years of drop-tower, parabolic-flight and shuttle droplet experiments. Published after critical review by skeptical reviewers. [SRC]
- Signature (slide): low heat release rate, quasi-steady burning, a second extinction, lower activation energy.
- Conditions: n-heptane in air at 1 atm; also 18% O2 in N2 (82%) and 18/67/15 O2-N2-CO2. Later tests show similar behavior for n-octane and n-decane. [SRC]
- Fire-safety implication [SRC, authors' interpretation]: the cool flame can persist after hot-flame extinction, generating partially oxidized, combustible vapor that can re-ignite, akin to smoldering in solid fuels. Recent results show re-ignition with decane. [SRC]
- Second-stage temperature debate [SRC, S5 intro]: Nayagam's analysis allowed 1000-1400 K for the second stage if heat release were 50%, but a true cool flame at the NTC maximum would sit near 700 K with heptyl ketohydroperoxide, formaldehyde and alkenes as main products instead of H2O, CO2 and CO. Simulation later gave about 750 K (FLEX-08).
- Independent support [SRC]: Cuoci, Frassoldati, Faravelli, Ranzi (Politecnico di Milano) reported cool-flame second-stage burning in simulations of the same case (21% O2, d0 = 3.91 mm).
- Why the classical mechanism needs care [SRC, S5]: low-temperature oxidation chemistry (R + O2 to RO2 to QOOH to O2QOOH to ketohydroperoxide + OH) normally needs partial premixing, so a diffusive low-temperature flame was surprising.

### [CHUNK FLEX-08] Numerical modelling of the cool flame | source: S5, S3 | tags: simulation, kinetics, heptane, radiation, parametric
Model [SRC]: transient 1-D spherosymmetric droplet code with detailed gas-phase kinetics, spectral radiation and multicomponent transport.
Kinetics [SRC]: Curran et al. n-heptane mechanism (1038 species, 2739 reactions) reduced by path flux analysis (PFA) to 128 species and 565 reactions; reproduces shock-tube ignition delay (1, 13.5, 30 atm) and flow-reactor oxidation (8 atm) including the NTC region. A high-temperature-only mechanism (Chaos et al. 2007) is used as a control.
Base case [SRC]: d0 = 3.91 mm, 21% O2 / 79% N2, 1 atm.
- High-temperature-only model: radiative extinction at large size, then pure evaporation; extinguishes earlier than experiment.
- Detailed model: radiative extinction (first stage), then a second stage with significantly higher burning rate and a flame hugging the droplet at about 750 K, then extinction near the end. First-stage peak temperature near 2000 K. Reproduces experiment qualitatively. [SRC]
- Quantitative gap [SRC]: second-stage burning rate is over-predicted and extinction diameter under-predicted: about 0.35 mm, a factor of 3.5 below experiment (so experiment is about 1.2 mm [CALC]).
- Heat budget (S5 Fig. 4) [SRC, numbers FIG]: Q_generation spikes to about 380 W at ignition, falls to about 100 W by the end of stage 1; Q_radiation plateaus near 85 W and Q_conduction near 38 W, so radiation is about 2x conduction in stage 1. Transition to stage 2 when total losses meet generation (about 6-7 s in simulation). Stage-2 generation is about 17 W (about 11% of stage 1), and the dominant loss switches from radiation to conduction.
- Mechanism of transition [SRC]: heat loss (not radiation specifically) moves the flame close to the droplet and drops temperature into the cool-flame window.
- Parametric studies (all n-heptane, 1 atm) [SRC, details FIG]:
  - Initial diameter 2-7 mm in air: larger d0 gives an earlier transition; 2 and 3 mm stay single-stage, 4 mm and above go two-stage.
  - CO2 added to a 3.0 mm droplet: 0% CO2 single-stage; 5% to 70% CO2 triggers the cool flame, and more CO2 means earlier transition (about 0.8 s/mm^2 at 5% down to about 0.1 s/mm^2 at 30%+ [FIG]).
  - He added to a 3.0 mm droplet: also triggers the transition earlier, via enhanced conductive loss. Initial burning rate rises (up to about 0.9 mm^2/s at 70% He [FIG]), but the second stage ends sooner and a larger residual droplet remains [FIG, INF].
- Kinetic tuning (S3) [SRC]: Curran chemistry with PFA reduction; "revised" model changed two sensitive rates: QOOHO2 to QOOH + O2 (A factor x2) and QOOHO2 to ketohydroperoxide + OH (A factor /2). Revised kinetics improved ignition-delay and flow-reactor reactivity in the low-temperature region, a case where droplet data improves kinetics used by other methods. Conclusion: widely used detailed models do not accurately predict second-stage cool-flame extinction.
- Take-home [INF]: any enhanced heat loss (radiative CO2, conductive He, large size) can push a droplet into the cool-flame branch. This directly links FLEX suppressant studies to cool-flame hazard: suppression by dilution may convert a hot flame into a cool one rather than extinguishing it.

### [CHUNK FLEX-09] Initial-diameter effects: n-octane and n-decane | source: S4 | tags: droplet-size, soot, radiation, fiber, octane, decane
- Question [SRC]: how burning rate $K_0$ depends on initial diameter $D_0$ over the widest range ever done for one fuel.
- Range [SRC]: $0.52\le D_0\le 0.85$ mm in a ground 1.2 s drop tower (fibers 14 um SiC); $2.16\le D_0\le 4.97$ mm on ISS (MDCA). No data for 0.85-1.7 mm because drop-tower time is too short and ISS deployment near 1.5 mm could impart drift. Conditions: room-temperature air, 1 atm. Fuels n-octane (to 3.61 mm) and n-decane (to 4.97 mm). [SRC]
- MDCA method [SRC]: fuel pushed through hollow needles into a liquid bridge, needles retracted fast, hot-wire igniters, free-floating or 80 um SiC-tethered droplets; Hi-Beam backlit camera (1 MP, 30 fps), color camera, and low-light UV camera for OH emission. Droplet, flame and soot-shell diameters extracted by image analysis (Dembia et al. 2012 Matlab tool).
- Findings [SRC]:
  1. $K$ and FSR decrease with increasing $D_0$ in every time interval; SSR increases with $D_0$.
  2. Small droplets (0.52-0.85 mm; radiation negligible): lower $K$ with larger $D_0$, attributed to more soot and longer fuel residence time.
  3. Large droplets (2.16-4.97 mm): $K$ still decreases, but the flame is less luminous (less soot), so the cause is increasing radiative loss reducing heat feedback to the droplet.
  4. Radiative extinction visible for octane at $D_0 = 3.61$ mm (about 1.0 s/mm^2) with a clear burning-rate drop; post-extinction burning is slower than before but still faster than pure evaporation. For decane with $D_0>3.97$ mm extinction is subtler (flame disappearance); pre-extinction $K$ is lower than octane, partly attributed to higher liquid density.
  5. After radiative extinction the soot shell keeps expanding while no new soot forms; suggested cause is weaker thermophoresis once the hot flame is gone.
  6. Fiber effect: the 80 um SiC fiber induces convection around ~1-2 mm droplets (flame displaced farther, higher $K$ and FSR); negligible for $D_0\approx 4.97$ mm. New idea: fibers may act through gas motion, not only heat conduction.
- Link to cool flames [INF]: the post-extinction burning rate being above pure evaporation in octane and decane is consistent with the second-stage burning in heptane (FLEX-07). The paper does not use the term "cool flame".

>>> source: RAG/Tamer.txt | chunk: FLEX-10 | location: lines 141-148 | mapping: FLEX deep analysis pack (file header: FLEX, PSI-69); header names no other experiment
### [CHUNK FLEX-10] Methanol: water absorption, evaporation, extinction | source: S6 | tags: methanol, water, extinction, OH-star, ZGF, CO2
- Why methanol [SRC]: simple kinetics, almost no soot, small flame standoff (minimal radiation effects), and combustion water condenses on the droplet, a model for bi-component fuels.
- Mixing limits [SRC]: diffusion-limited (thin water boundary layer, evaporates early with the fuel) vs convection-limited (homogeneous droplet, more water, more water in the vapor).
- ISS FLEX methanol tests [SRC]: O2 13-21% with CO2/N2 diluents, 1 atm. Plot of extinction diameter vs initial diameter forms two clusters: 13-16% O2 near the no-burn line (little burning before extinction), 18-21% O2 much smaller extinction diameters. [FIG, INF]
- Example ISS test FLEX-145 [SRC, with conflict]: slide 10: P = 763.5 mmHg, Y_O2 0.199, Y_N2 0.749, Y_CO2 0.050, $D_0$ = 3.33 mm, $D_{ext}$ = 1.613 mm, $K_{avg}$ = 0.448 mm^2/s; date 2010-11-16. Slide 9 gives conflicting composition and size (see FLEX-13).
- Ground (ZGF drop tower) tests [SRC]: 16 methanol tests, 21% O2 with Ar/N2 diluents, 0.5-2 atm. Ar/N2 mimics CO2/N2 without gas-phase radiation. $D_0$ about 1.5-2.0 mm gave $d_e$ about 0.65-1.05 mm, nearly linear [FIG]. Example H-8-04: 1 atm, 21% O2 / 35% Ar / 44% N2, $D_0$ = 1.69 mm, $D_{ext}$ = 0.79 mm.
- Method [SRC]: OH* chemiluminescence from the Low-Light-Level Ultra-Violet (LLUV) camera in the ISS runs; blue-flame pixel intensity from the 8-bit color camera in the ZGF. Flame intensity falls when water starts to evaporate (about 3 s in H-8-04); this marks the water-flux transition diameter $d_c$ (condensation to evaporation). $d_c$ (about 0.75-1.8 mm) sits above $d_e$ in the ZGF data [FIG]. Summary: flame-intensity analysis gives the water-flux transition point; a color camera may be an adequate substitute.
- Future work [SRC]: extend analysis to the full FLEX methanol data set, refine correlations, compare with theory.

### [CHUNK FLEX-11] Publications corpus (PSI list) | source: S1 | tags: publications, corpus, bibliography
- The PSI record lists 51 entries (my count) [CALC]. Most have DOIs; several do not (e.g. "Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity", "Methanol Droplet Extinction in Oxygen/Carbon-dioxide/Nitrogen Mixtures...", "FLEX: A Decisive Step Forward...", "Dynamics of Water Absorption and Evaporation...", Ghata & Shaw "Computational modeling of the effects of support fibers...", and the "Detailed results from FLEX" report).
- Theme clusters (approximate, by title) [INF]:
  - Methanol / alcohol droplets and water effects (Nayagam, Hicks, Shaw, Farouk & Dryer, Williams).
  - Cool flames and n-alkane two-stage burning (Nayagam et al. 2012, 2015, 2016; Farouk & Dryer 2014; Paczko, Peters, Seshadri, Williams; Prince, Williams, Ovando).
  - Support-fiber effects (Ghata & Shaw; Shringi, Dwyer & Shaw; Liu, Xu, Avedisian, Hicks).
  - Fuel surrogates, biofuels, gasoline (Avedisian group: methyl decanoate/butanoate, Jet-A, camelina, tallow, n-butanol, indolene).
  - Propanol, heptane/methanol and heptane/ethanol mixtures, and sub-millimeter droplets in drop towers (Shaw group). These are ground-based, so not all PSI-69 publications come from ISS data.
  - Methods: image analysis (Dembia et al.), backlit-image interpretation (Yu & Shaw), uncertainties (Shaw 2014), needle-retraction flow simulations (Jin & Shaw), droplet LIF/spectroscopy.
  - Overview papers: Dietrich et al. "Droplet Combustion Experiments Aboard the ISS" (DOI 10.1007/s12217-014-9372-2); "Detailed results from FLEX, March 2009 to December 2011" (Dietrich et al.; likely NASA/TP-2013-216046, cited as [1] in S5 [FLAG]).
- Use: the supplied talks and papers (S3-S6) are probably related to entries here (e.g. S4 to "Experimental Study of Initial Diameter Effects...", S5 to "Isolated n-heptane droplet combustion in microgravity: Cool Flames", S6 to "Dynamics of Water Absorption and Evaporation...", S3 to the Nayagam cool-flame papers). The mapping is inferred from titles, not confirmed. [INF]

>>> source: RAG/Tamer.txt | chunk: FLEX-12 | location: lines 162-170 | mapping: FLEX deep analysis pack (file header: FLEX, PSI-69); header names no other experiment
### [CHUNK FLEX-12] Cross-source synthesis and insights | source: all | tags: insights, synthesis
1. Heat loss is the control variable. Radiation (large droplet, CO2) and conduction (He) both drive the transition from hot flame to cool flame (S5), and radiative loss controls burning-rate decline at large size (S4). One mechanism ties the suppressant tests (S7) to the cool-flame discovery (S3).
2. Suppression by dilution may not be complete extinction. CO2 and He at modest levels push heptane droplets into a cool-flame branch with persistent vapor generation and possible re-ignition (S3, S5). Fire-safety margins should therefore be set by the end of the cool-flame stage, not just the loss of visible flame. [INF]
3. Microgravity changes suppressant ranking. N2 is far less effective in micro-g by MEC (0.26 to 0.38), CO2 less so (0.16 to 0.19); other studies conflict (S7). FLEX was designed to resolve this with droplets at controlled pressure and O2.
4. Visible-flame extinction is not the end of reactions. Post-extinction burning in octane and decane stays above pure-evaporation rates (S4), heptane shows a second stage (S3), and kinetic models underpredict extinction size (S5). [INF]
5. Fiber artifacts matter. Support fibers can drive micro-convection (S4), so free-droplet data are the cleaner dataset for model validation; fiber data need correction. [INF]
6. Methanol is the calibration fuel, heptane the discovery fuel. Methanol shows classical radiative/diffusive extinction plus water effects (S6); heptane shows anomalous behavior (S3, S5). Combining them gives a validation ladder for kinetics.
7. Model-readiness is high. Droplet data are small, 1-D and well characterized, and kinetics were tuned with them (S3). This supports the dashboard score model=3. [INF]
8. Dashboard relevance [INF, subjective]: FLEX strongly supports Suppression (3) and Model-ready data (3). Its relevance to Detection is nil. The seed hiO2=1 is plausible: LOI and suppressant tests run mostly at 10-40% O2, not high-O2 cabins. The cool-flame re-ignition finding may justify raising Prevention above 1; this is a judgment, not data.

### [CHUNK FLEX-13] Data-quality flags | source: S1-S7 | tags: data-quality, flags, verify
- F1 [FLAG] S6 slide 9 (FLEX-145): "20% O2 / 75% CO2 / 5% N2, $D_0$ = 3.38 mm, $D_{ext}$ = 1.66" conflicts with slide 10: Y_CO2 = 0.050, Y_N2 = 0.749, $D_0$ = 3.330 mm, $D_{ext}$ = 1.613 mm. Slide 10 matches the data box on the plot. Treat slide 10 as primary and CO2/N2 on slide 9 as likely swapped.
- F2 [FLAG] S6 slides 7 and 9 give burning rate "K = 0.67 m^2/s" and "0.44 m^2/s". Units must be mm^2/s (slide 10 uses mm^2/s: 0.448).
- F3 [FLAG] S5 figure captions: Fig. 5 caption lists burning rate as (b) and flame standoff as (c), but panel (b) plots FSR and panel (c) plots K. Same swap in Fig. 6 and 7. Also Fig. 3 caption says "(b) burning rate, (c) flame radius" while panel (b) is flame diameter and (c) burning rate.
- F4 [FLAG] S5 (dated May 2013) cites reference [1] "NASA/TP-2013-216046 ... December 2013". Date is inconsistent; the manuscript may have been updated, or the date is a typo.
- F5 [FLAG] S4 text cross-references "Figs. 10b-e and 11b-e" for fiber data; likely Figs. 9 and 10. Abstract says ISS handled $D_0>1.2$ mm while Methods say $D_0>1.7$ mm; the reported data start at 2.16 mm.
- F6 [FLAG] Suppressants: PSI text and S7 plan list CO2, He, SF6; S3 slide lists nitrogen, helium, CO2 and xenon. Confirm what was actually flown (xenon vs SF6).
- F7 [FLAG] Start date: PSI says 2007-08-01; S5 says ISS experiments began in 2009; "Detailed results" covers March 2009 to December 2011. Likely the earlier date is the award start, not the first ISS run.
- F8 [FLAG] S5 gives the predicted extinction diameter as about 0.35 mm, 3.5x smaller than experiment; no experimental value is stated, so the 1.2 mm in FLEX-08 is back-calculated.
- F9 [FLAG] Dashboard (S2): FLEX-2 has no PSI ID; BASS ID is "presumed"; SAME and others "third-party" unconfirmed. Verify on PSI before treating IDs as authoritative.
- F10 [FLAG] [FIG] values (temperatures, W, thresholds) are read from plots and are approximate (typically +/-10%).

### [CHUNK FLEX-15] Q&A pairs (for retrieval testing / few-shot) | tags: qa
Q: What is the DOI and PSI ID of FLEX? A: DOI 10.60555/mbq8-0451, PSI-69. [SRC]
Q: What hardware did FLEX use? A: MDCA inside the CIR of the FCF on ISS. [SRC]
Q: What does LOI mean and how does it relate to MEC? A: LOI is the lowest O2 mole fraction that supports a quasi-steady flame; $\mathrm{LOI}=0.209(1-\mathrm{MEC})$. [SRC]
Q: Is CO2 a better suppressant than He in microgravity? A: By cup-burner MEC (0.19 vs 0.31) yes, CO2 is more effective; Honda and Ronney's thin-solid flame spread results suggest the opposite. It depends on fuel and geometry. [SRC/INF]
Q: How many tests were planned and for which fuels? A: 290, split evenly between n-heptane and methanol (145 each). [CALC]
Q: What was surprising about the heptane droplets? A: After radiative extinction of the visible flame, they kept burning quasi-steadily via a low-temperature cool flame until a second extinction at a finite diameter. [SRC]
Q: What temperature does the simulated cool flame have? A: About 750 K, versus about 2000 K at the start of the hot-flame stage. [SRC/FIG]
Q: Why does a larger droplet transition to the cool-flame stage earlier? A: More radiative loss; heat loss moves the flame close to the droplet and cools it into the low-temperature window. [SRC]
Q: How does the initial droplet diameter affect the burning rate? A: Burning rate decreases as $D_0$ increases across 0.5-5 mm, due to soot and residence time when small and radiative loss when large. [SRC]
Q: Why is methanol used? A: Simple kinetics, almost no soot, small flame standoff, and water back-diffusion makes it a bi-component model. [SRC]
Q: Why does the methanol flame intensity drop during burning? A: Water that condensed starts evaporating with the fuel and cools the flame; this marks the water-flux transition diameter $d_c$. [SRC]
Q: Which numbers in the sources conflict? A: See FLEX-13 (FLEX-145 composition and size, units of K, figure captions, suppressant lists).
Q: Why does cool-flame burning matter for spacecraft fire safety? A: It generates combustible partially oxidized vapor and can re-ignite after the visible flame is gone, so flame loss does not guarantee safety. [SRC/INF]

### [CHUNK FLEX-23] FLEX Research Requirements Document (2005): design, requirements, success criteria
Source: S9 (S7 is an excerpt)
Tags: requirements, success-criteria, diagnostics, ground-program, justification

- Document: "Research Requirements Document: Droplet Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity (FLEX)", 4 Nov 2005, 81 pages (LaTeX). Research team lead F.A. Williams (UC San Diego); NASA members M. Hicks (GRC) and V. Nayagam (NCSER); external members M.Y. Choi (listed at Drexel University), F.L. Dryer (Princeton), B.D. Shaw (UC Davis). Sections: 1 Introduction, 2 Fire suppression background, 3 Droplet combustion for fire-suppression research, 4 Flight experiment description, 5 Flight experiment requirements and test matrix, 6 Post-flight analysis and success criteria, 7 Ground program, 8 Management, 9 Justification for reduced gravity, Appendix A previous droplet experiments (FSDC, FSDC-2, DCE, soot and Soret ground studies). [SRC]
- Context [SRC]: ISS US segment uses CO2 extinguishers, Russian modules water-based foam. Suppressant choice criteria in the 1985 and 1990 trade studies: effectiveness, reliability, maintainability, system weight, post-fire cleanup, toxicity, collateral damage. NASA FPDS suppression objectives: (i) suppressant effectiveness in reduced gravity, (ii) large-scale agent deployment, (iii) verify suppression-system design rules. Without buoyancy, suppressant transport, diffusion, thermophoresis and radiation dominate. Crew motion or extinguisher discharge can create flows of several cm/s (up to about 50 cm/s locally in a rack, Wu and Ruff 2003), which motivates the slow-flow tests.
- Flammability theory [SRC]: S-curve of flame temperature vs Damkohler number (Fendell 1972); Linan (1974) extinction criterion `δe = τch/τr = f(1-|γ|)` with an oxidizer-mass-fraction and temperature dependence (formula garbled in extraction) [FLAG]; Table 1 lists reduced Damkohler numbers for droplet combustion (Law 1975), stagnation-point boundary layer (Wu et al. 1982) and rotating disk (Nayagam and Williams 2000), each containing `(Tf/Ta)^3 exp(-Ta/Tf)` [INF, reconstructed from garbled text].
- Buoyancy justification [SRC/CALC]: sphericity needs diffusive residence times short vs buoyant time: `τk/τb = sqrt(gD^3)/αg` and `τm/τb = sqrt(gD^3)/Dg` (both much below 1; `αg` = thermal and `Dg` = mass diffusivity of the gas). `Gr/Re² = gβΔT D/U∞²` much below 1. Worst case `ΔT ≈ 5 K`, `D ≈ 1 cm`, `U ≈ 1 cm/s` gives required `g/g0 ≈ 10^-5`, i.e. below `10^-4 m/s²` (`10^-4/9.81 = 1.0×10^-5`). Check with `β = 1/300 K^-1`: `Gr/Re² = 16 × (g/g0)`, so `10^-5` gives `1.6×10^-4`. [CALC] 1-g tests at 1 atm would need D far below 1 mm, where extinction diameters are unmeasurable; reduced pressure at 1 g (Chung and Law 1986) covers too narrow a range, and Easton (1998) found that conditions with finite extinction diameter at 1 g burn to completion in microgravity. The 10 s JAMIC drop tower used by Dietrich et al. 2005 is no longer available.
- Independent variables (Section 4.2 and Table 4) [SRC]: O2 0.10-0.40; suppressants CO2, He, SF6 at 0-0.70 (0.70 expected for the weakest agent); pressure 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 atm; fuels n-heptane (sooting alkane) and methanol (non-sooting alcohol with bound oxygen, small standoff); D0 2-6 mm (3 and 5 mm in the matrix); slow flow 0.1-5 cm/s by translating the fiber. DCE-1 (earlier flight, He diluent, same fuels) is the baseline.
- Hardware requirements (Table 4) [SRC]: fuel research grade, dry, degassed, purity above 99.5%, 18-27 C; droplet tolerance +/-0.25 mm, reproducibility +/-5%; fiber under 100 um; hot-wire igniter at 1-5 radii from the surface (0.5-2.5 D0), 0.5 mm positioning, igniter on 1-5 s; exclusion zone cylinder 20 D0 downstream, 8 D0 upstream, 10 D0 diameter; pressure +/-0.05 atm, held within +/-10% during a test; gas tolerance +/-0.005 (O2) and +/-0.01 (others); humidity below 10% (heptane) and below 2% (methanol); settle 2 min after fill; dwell at least 10 s before ignition; fuel vapor below 0.005; CO, CO2 and products below 0.02 (each) in atmospheres without CO2.
- Diagnostics (Table 5) [SRC]: droplet backlit view FOV 3 cm, 30 um, 30 fps, DOF 3 cm, optional 2x2 binned 60-100 fps at 60 um; OH* at 310 nm +/-5 nm, FOV 5 cm, 100 um, 30 fps; color camera FOV 5 cm, 100 um, 30 fps, near-real-time downlink; radiometers 0.6-5.0 um broadband and 1.87 um water-vapor narrow band, 30 Hz, accuracy 5% of full scale, time constant below 40 ms, at least 15 cm from the droplet, FOV 65 mm; soot volume fraction 660 nm backlight (FWHM 5 nm), 50 um, at least 5 cm FOV; soot/fiber temperature two-color LCTF pyrometry; flow velocity sampling 30 Hz; pressure/temperature 10 Hz, +/-0.01 atm, +/-0.5 C; GMT sync +/-0.03 s.
- Science end products (Table 3) [SRC]: 1a Dext vs O2 and pressure; 1b LOI vs pressure; 1c transient effects; 2a-2c LOI, Dext and heat release/radiation vs suppressant; 3 validated numerical models; 4a-4e reduced sub-models (radiation, kinetics with suppressants, soot, transport with Soret diffusion, small sub-buoyant flows).
- Flight procedure (Section 5.3) is the 8-step LOI procedure in FLEX-04; the S8 table follows it with ladders (FLEX-17).
- Success criteria (Section 6.2) [SRC]. Minimal: (1) droplet diameter plus OH* or color flame video vs time for both fuels at two pressures over a range of sizes and O2 to define LOI; (2) same with slow flow near extinction for at least 5 droplets; (3) both fuels, one pressure, two O2 levels, four CO2 fractions; (4) same with one more suppressant (He or SF6); (5) slow flow for at least 10 droplets with suppressants; (6) radiometric data at two pressures, two O2, four CO2 fractions; (7) soot volume fraction, temperature and radiometer data at P = 3 atm, O2 = 0.21 and two CO2 levels (Table 12). Complete: all diagnostics for all tests, at least four pressures, three pressures x four O2 levels, at least three suppressants, slow flow for at least 10 droplets with one quarter including soot data, soot data at three pressures and four O2 levels, and soot data for two pressures, two O2 levels and four suppressant levels. Not every test point has to succeed for Complete Success if all objectives are covered. Check against S8 in FLEX-18.
- Data policy [SRC]: archive raw images, camera settings, scale factors, radiometer data, housekeeping data in an open format such as HDF; GRC investigators responsible; public within 2 years of flight completion. Raw droplet history is derived from backlit images (Choi et al. 1989; Struk et al. 1998 methods).
- Ground program (Section 7) [SRC]: 2.2 s and 5.2 s GRC drop towers (including slow-flow rigs at 0-3 cm/s and D 1-3 mm), UC Davis high-pressure rigs, Drexel soot rig, Princeton, and GRC rigs to set the final matrix; Dryer leads detailed modeling (heptane, methanol, ethanol mechanisms, soot sub-models, inert substitution studies with CO2, He, SF6; Kroenlein et al. 2004); Shaw leads fiber-supported droplet modeling (overset grids: main cylindrical grid, droplet grid, fiber grid; Marangoni flows).
- Management (Section 8) [SRC]: Williams has overall responsibility; Nayagam and Hicks run flight-hardware work; Dryer owns the numerical model.
- Internal inconsistencies of S9 are listed in flag F16 (FLEX-13).

### [CHUNK FLEX-25] CIR imaging diagnostics: capabilities and derived numbers
Source: S11 (CIR-DOC-4064), S9, S10
Tags: CIR, diagnostics, HiBMs, LLL-UV, imaging, calc

**Capabilities [SRC], CIR Payload Accommodations Handbook, 1 Oct 2008:**

| Package | Use | Spectral band | FOV | Resolution | Frame rate | Record time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HiBMs (telecentric, 12-bit, 1024x1024) | droplet backlit view, soot volume fraction, soot temperature, shadowgraph | 650-1050 nm via LCTF (10 nm bandpass), removable | 30, 50, 90 mm | about 10 lp/mm = 0.050 mm | up to 30 fps full frame; 60 fps at 512x512 binned | about 18 min at 30 fps; about 36 min at 60 fps |
| LLL-UV (Gen II MCP intensifier, 18 mm) | OH* at 310 nm | filter 310 nm, 10 nm FWHM; sensor 250-750 nm, peak 450 nm | 50 mm square (80 mm with deferred hardware) | 3.6 lp/mm = 0.138 mm (binned) | 7.5, 15, 30 fps full frame; 54 fps binned | about 18 min at 30 fps; about 40 min at 54 fps |
| LLL-IR | CH* at 430 nm | filter module changeable | 50 mm | 4.5 lp/mm = 0.110 mm (binned) | 30 fps full; 54 fps binned | same as LLL-UV |
| Illumination package | collimated backlight | 650-660 nm, bandwidth under 10 nm, laser diode used below lasing threshold | 90 mm beam, divergence 0.339 deg | 8-bit programmable output (0-255) | CW | - |

- Other CIR items [SRC]: Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS) attenuates vibration above about 1 Hz without ISS resources; SAMS tri-axial sensor head on the Optics Bench measures accelerations; Diagnostic packages mount on the Optics Bench through common flange mounts.
- Derived numbers [CALC]:
  - Pixel pitch = FOV/pixels: HiBMs 30 mm / 1024 = 29.3 um, 50 mm = 48.8 um, 90 mm = 87.9 um; binned 512 px: 58.6, 97.7, 175.8 um. So the S9/S10 droplet requirement of 30 um over a 3 cm FOV equals the HiBMs 30 mm full-frame mode, and the 60 um at 60-100 fps requirement equals the 30 mm binned mode (58.6 um).
  - LLL-UV: 50 mm / 512 binned = 97.7 um, 50 mm / 1024 = 48.8 um. The OH requirement of 100 um (S9) is met by binned mode only if the stated 0.138 mm is ignored; the handbook figure 0.138 mm (lp/mm basis) does not meet 100 um, whereas S10 relaxed it to 150 um, which 0.138 mm does meet. [CALC/INF]
  - Storage: the recording times imply the same buffer size in every mode: 1024x1024 x 12 bit (1.5 byte) x 30 fps x 18 min = 32,400 frames x 1.57 MB = about 51 GB; 512x512 x 1.5 byte x 60 fps x 36 min = 129,600 frames x 0.39 MB = about 51 GB; LLL-UV binned 54 fps x 40 min = 129,600 frames = about 51 GB. So the direct-to-disk buffer is about 51 GB per camera if data are packed at 12 bit. [CALC/INF]
  - Frame budget for a typical test: median burn 9.6 s at 30 fps = about 290 frames per camera, plus 10 s pre-ignition dwell and post-extinction time. [CALC]
- Flags [FLAG]:
  1. S9/S10 ask for 60-100 fps in binned mode, but the handbook gives up to 60 fps (HiBMs binned). The text on sub-frame readout is cut off in the excerpt, so a higher rate may exist for windowed readout. Unverified.
  2. LCTF switching time is 100 ms per the handbook, while two-color pyrometry needs at least 7 fps per wavelength with alternating frames (14 fps total, a 71 ms frame period). The two numbers conflict unless switching overlaps readout. Unverified. [INF]
  3. The handbook lists illumination uniformity as 60% and output as "less than 5 maw", apparently typographical (mW).
  4. The handbook is a 2008 document; the as-flown CIR configuration may differ.

### [CHUNK FLEX-26] Requirement evolution: FLEX (2005) vs FLEX-2 (2010)
Source: S9, S10, S11

|---|---|---|---|

| Color view | 100 um, DOF 3 cm | 100 um, DOF 5 mm | relaxed |

| Number of planned tests | 290 envelope (FLEX-06) | SRD 550 points; preliminary matrix 456 | FLEX-28 |

- S10 internal conflicts [FLAG]: igniter 30 AWG, 4 mm loops (3.4.1.2.4) vs 26 AWG, 75.8 mm, 1 ohm (4.2.3.2); bead spacing 12 and 24 mm (4.1.18) vs 12 mm (4.1.23); fiber 235 mm long (S10) vs 229 mm (S11); fiber rotation 68 degrees (S10) vs about 120 degrees (S11); droplet range 1.5-5 mm (S10) vs matrix sizes 3-5 mm; S10 lists flow 0.1-5 cm/s but matrix uses 0.1-0.5 cm/s.
- Reading [INF]: the FLEX-2 requirements are a relaxed, de-risked version of FLEX (imaging depth of field and OH resolution loosened, mixtures and arrays added) built on hardware already verified in FLEX.

### [CHUNK FLEX-29] Agent toolbox: formulas, filters and data schema
Source: S8, S9, S11
Tags: agent, tools, formulas, schema, python

- Use these exact definitions when computing from the flight table (`FLEX_flight_tests_clean.csv`).
- LOI and MEC: `LOI = 0.209(1-MEC)`, `MEC = 1-LOI/0.209`. At 0.7 atm the flight ladders use base O2 0.30 (30/70 N2), so use `xs = 1-xO2/0.30` there. [CALC]
- Equivalent dilution: `equiv_dilution = 1 - x_O2/0.209` (column in the clean CSV).
- Partial pressure: `pi = xi P` (atm), with P = `pressure_mmHg/760`.
- Extinction fraction: `Dext_over_D0 = Dext/D0`; near-limit if Extinction and `Dext_over_D0` at least 0.9.
- Average burning rate from table: `K_est = (D0^2-Dext^2)/t_burn` (matches the tabulated K within 15% in 87% of tests, FLEX-17).
- d-square law: `D^2 = D0^2-Kt`; droplet lifetime `τ = D0^2/K`.
- Droplet volume: `V = πD^3/6` (mm^3; 1 mL = 1000 mm^3).
- Image pixel pitch: FOV/pixels; frame storage = pixels x bits/8 x fps x seconds.
- Gas balance: `x_N2 = 1-x_O2-x_CO2-x_He` (sums to 1 within 0.015 except tests 69, 75, 76, 79, 80, 81).
- Schema of `FLEX_flight_tests_clean.csv` (274 rows, 24 columns): `test_no`, `flex_id`, `date`, `gmt`, `fuel`, `pressure_mmHg`, `pressure_atm`, `pressure_band`, `x_O2`, `x_N2`, `x_CO2`, `x_He`, `diluent`, `suppressant_fraction`, `equiv_dilution_1_minus_xO2_over_0.209`, `D0_mm`, `Dext_mm`, `Dext_over_D0`, `burning_rate_mm2_s`, `burn_time_s`, `burn_time_approx`, `test_end`, `id_group`, `flags`.
- Flags values: disruption_no_extinction_data 61, Dext_missing 49, Dext_corrupt_byte 28, K_missing 16, Dext_zero_no_visible_extinction 8, D0_missing 6, D0_corrupt_byte 6, composition_sum_off 6, duplicate_id 2, burn_time_approx 2, pressure_zero_invalid 1, Dext_gt_D0 1, K_implausibly_low 1. [CALC]
- Usable subsets: 159 Extinction tests with Dext > 0 (for extinction-diameter analysis); 262 tests with D0; 258 with K. Always drop `pressure_zero_invalid` (test 114) and treat Disruption rows as outcome-only.
- Agent behaviors recommended [INF]: (1) answer numeric questions by filtering the CSV, not from memory; (2) when asked for LOI say that no no-ignition test exists in the table and give the near-limit bracket from FLEX-19; (3) always state n for any ladder row; (4) when a question mixes FLEX and FLEX-2, check FLEX-24/26 first.
- Example filters (pandas):
  - Heptane, 1 atm, CO2: `df[(df.fuel=="heptane")&(df.pressure_band=="1.0atm")&(df.diluent=="CO2")]`
  - Near-limit set: `df[(df.test_end=="extinction")&(df.Dext_over_D0>=0.9)]`

### [CHUNK FLEX-30] Public web corroboration
Source: S13
Tags: web, press, corroboration, FLEX-2, media

Retrieved 2026-11-15. Paraphrased; no dates were shown in the retrieved text unless stated. Press accuracy is lower than the NASA documents, so use these only as corroboration.

- NBC News (about FLEX-2, labeled as "this month"): NASA's Daniel Dietrich and Forman Williams operate the experiment by remote control in the Destiny module; the team says methanol and heptane flames burn down to about 12-13% O2. This matches the table minimum (O2 0.12 methanol, 0.13 heptane, FLEX-19). The article calls it FLEX-2 although the result is a FLEX (this PSI record) result. [SRC/CALC][FLAG: naming]
- Smithsonian (Air & Space), "Great balls of floating fire": FLEX-2 runs in the 560-pound CIR in the Destiny module; the PI is Forman Williams; astronauts did four to 10 droplet burns per session, twice a week; the video shows a heptane droplet in a short hot flame, then a steady cool flame, then extinction in a bright orange vapor cloud. FLEX-2 is described as "more science-oriented" and tied to fuel mixtures for efficient engines. Consistent with S8 session sizes (median 3, maximum 9 tests per day). [SRC][FLAG: naming]
- Smithsonian (science and nature), jellyfish flames: FLEX-2 droplets of about 3 mm made of equal parts isooctane and heptane show pulsing "jellyfish" flames only for droplets of about 3 mm or larger and not always; Thomas Avedisian (Cornell) is a co-investigator; cool-flame combustion is cited as relevant to cleaner engines. [SRC]
- Gizmodo: co-investigator Vedha Nayagam says helium, carbon dioxide and "sometimes" xenon were tried as inert ambient gases to find the most effective suppressant. Xenon does not appear in S8. [SRC][F6]
- phys.org / NASA (Sept 2014): astronaut Reid Wiseman ran FLEX-2 and described a "jellyfish of fire"; Williams explains disruptive soot burning; Avedisian leads that study of burning rates and soot agglomeration. NASA Scientific Visualization Studio "Spherical Flames" (16 Sept 2014) also covers FLEX-2. [SRC]
- LabXchange: FLEX-2 is the second FLEX experiment using fuels and conditions closer to real combustors. [SRC]
- Low-reliability page (an education blog) claims FLEX-2 tested new suppression agents and ventilation techniques; this is not supported by S10 or S11 (N2/He only) and should be ignored. [FLAG]
- Conclusions [INF]: FLEX-2 flew on ISS (at least through 2014); its public emphasis is fuel mixtures, soot and cool flames, not CO2 suppression; press mixes FLEX and FLEX-2 names, so rely on S8 for FLEX data.

### [CHUNK FLEX-31] Cross-source insights, version 2
Source: all
Tags: insights, synthesis, v2

1. The flight ladders make LOI a direct dilution test. At 1 atm the CO2 and He ladders hold O2/N2 at air ratio and add suppressant, so the suppressant fraction equals MEC in `LOI = 0.209(1-MEC)`. The experiment therefore measures MEC for each fuel and agent directly. [CALC]
2. Droplet and cup-burner limits agree for heptane, not for methanol. Heptane near-limit CO2 0.19-0.20 and N2 0.38 equal the microgravity cup-burner MEC (0.19, 0.38). Methanol needs CO2 about 0.33-0.36 and He about 0.38 (N2 not reached above 0.43). Agent design margins depend on fuel; an oxygenated fuel is harder to suppress with CO2. [CALC/INF]
3. CO2 lowers and He raises burning rate at fixed O2 (`K He > CO2`, p < 0.01 in both fuels), so a suppressant changes heat release, not only the limit; this also fits the simulation of S5 where He raises initial K and brings the cool-flame stage earlier. [CALC/INF]
4. Yield: 186 of 274 tests (68%) ended in Extinction and 159 (58%) have a measured Dext. Disruption (22%) removes most high-O2 and 0.7 atm high-O2 tests (15 of 17 at O2 0.30-0.34). Plan any new extinction study at O2 below 0.22. [CALC]
5. The table mixes extinction stages. In heptane in air the shortest runs end near 0.8 D0 (hot-flame radiative extinction), while a 17.5 s run ends at 1.37 mm, close to the second-stage size implied by S5. Any model-validation use of Dext must split first-stage from second-stage extinction. [INF]
6. Heat loss is still the control variable: lower pressure shifts the near-limit O2 fraction up (0.7 atm vs 1 atm: lowest O2 with a flame 0.15 vs 0.14 methanol, 0.17 vs 0.17 heptane; near-limit pO2 about 0.12-0.14 vs 0.15-0.18 atm) while partial pressure of CO2 at the methanol limit is the same (0.32 atm). A partial-pressure framing might unify limits across pressures for methanol; not for heptane. [INF, weak]
7. FLEX is a suppression experiment; FLEX-2 is a combustion-chemistry experiment. Dropped CO2/SF6, added fuel mixtures, droplet arrays, flow velocities 0.1-0.5 cm/s and OH/soot diagnostics. The cool-flame discovery in FLEX likely shaped the FLEX-2 emphasis (web articles). [INF]
8. Highest-value open items for fire safety: (a) the 2-3 atm radiative corner has only 9 tests at one condition (CO2 0.70); (b) SF6 and xenon are absent; (c) flow-velocity identification is missing from S8; (d) no "no ignition" bracket for LOI; (e) He heptane ladder stops at O2 0.16. [CALC]
9. Dashboard scoring (S2 row FLEX: [prev 1, det 0, sup 3, hiO2 1, hab 2, model 3]) [INF, subjective]: S8 supports model = 3 (274 tests with D0, Dext, K, burn time) and sup = 3 (CO2/He/N2 limits). hiO2 = 1 stays reasonable (flown O2 at most 0.34, and tests above O2 0.26 mostly end by disruption). The FLEX-2 row [1, 0, 3, 1, 2, 3] copies FLEX; S10 suggests sup should be lower (2) because CO2 is absent and the focus is fuels; this is a judgment, not data.
10. Verified cross-checks: S6 slide 10 test 145 equals S8 row 145 exactly; press-quoted 12-13% O2 limits equal S8 minima; session sizes in the press match S8 test-day counts; storage arithmetic of the CIR cameras is self-consistent (about 51 GB). [CALC]

### [CHUNK FLEX-17] Flight test table: provenance and data dictionary
Source: S8
Tags: data, csv, dictionary, flight-data

- Source S8: `PSI-69_Experimental_table_FLEX.csv` (PSI "Experimental table" folder). 274 test rows, 15 columns. Cleaned copy with per-row flags: `FLEX_flight_tests_clean.csv` (24 columns). [SRC][CALC]
- Dates: first test 2009-03-05 (test 1, id 20CAL08), last 2011-12-08 (test 274). Matches the "Detailed results, March 2009 to December 2011" report window. [CALC]
- Fuels: methanol 157 tests, n-heptane 117. Diluents: N2-only 101, CO2/N2 123, He/N2 50. No SF6 or xenon columns exist. [CALC]
- Columns [SRC]: FLEX Test #, FLEX Identifier, Test Date, Test GMT, Fuel, Ambient pressure (mmHg), O / N / CO / He initial ambient mole fractions, Droplet initial diameter (mm), Visible flame extinction diameter (mm), Burning rate (mm), Burn time (s), Test end.
- Header quirks [INF]: "CO" almost certainly means CO2 (fractions 0.05-0.70; O2+N2+CO sums to 1). "Burning rate; mm" must be mm^2/s (values 0.25-1.06 match K in mm^2/s of S6). The CSV is Windows-1252, not UTF-8; 34 cells hold a corrupt byte instead of a number.
- Test end values [SRC]: Extinction 186, Disruption 61, Completion 27. Interpretation [INF]: Extinction = visible flame went out at a finite diameter; Completion = droplet burned out; Disruption = test ended by droplet disruption, so no extinction diameter is available.
- Identifier prefixes [CALC/INF]: C## = CO2-diluent conditions (108 tests), H## = helium (50), N## = N2-only (23); numeric prefixes (e.g. 20CAL08, 256F002, 192F001) = earlier and calibration tests (93). The trailing F or R before the 3-digit run number is undecoded: R tests have smaller mean D0 (2.74 mm, 25 tests) than F tests (3.27 mm, 59 tests). Meaning unverified. [FLAG]
- Visible-flame extinction diameter 0 appears in tests ending Completion and Disruption; read it as "no visible-flame extinction before test end". [INF]
- Derived columns in the clean CSV: `pressure_atm`, `pressure_band` (0.7, 1.0, 2-3 atm), `diluent`, `suppressant_fraction`, `equiv_dilution = 1-x_O2/0.209`, `Dext_over_D0`, `id_group`, `flags`.

FLX-REQ-0001
                                                                               February 04, 2010

PREFACE

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has developed a modular, multi-
user experimentation mini-facility for conducting droplet combustion science experiments in the
microgravity environment of the International Space Station (ISS). This facility, called the
Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), resides in Combustion Integrated Rack
(CIR), a component of the Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF) on-board the ISS. The Flame
Extinguishment Experiment 2 (FLEX-2) uses the MDCA platform to conduct droplet
combustion tests.

This document will define the engineering and science requirements necessary to successfully
complete the FLEX-2 experiments.

1.0            INTRODUCTION

1.1            Purpose
This document will define the engineering requirements necessary to successfully complete the
science and safety requirements. This document will be used by the FLEX-2 design engineers to
develop the systems necessary for FLEX-2. Interface and carrier requirements levied on FLEX-
2 are documented in the CIR-MDCA Interface Control Document (FCF-ICD-CIR-MDCA).
FLEX-2 will use the existing Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) hardware and
software platform already developed as a baseline for meeting many of the requirements found in
this document. Safety requirements are documented in the CIR/MDCA Integrated Hazard
Reports and the MDCA Hazard Reports (Re-Flight).

1.2            Scope
This FLEX-2 Engineering Requirements Document (ERD) serves to document two sets of
requirements: Science Requirements and Derived Engineering Requirements. The FLEX-2
Science Requirements Document (SRD) is created by the experiment’s Principle Investigators
(PI’s) and defines the requirements that are necessary to accomplish the FLEX-2 science
objectives. The purpose of this document is to provide traceability to the SRD and to formalize
these requirements. Also, it defines the engineering requirements derived to establish the
capabilities for a system that achieves the science requirements in conjunction with existing CIR
and MDCA capabilities.

1                FLEX-2 Engineering Requirements

publications. These documents have been grouped into two categories: applicable documents
and reference documents.

2.1            Order of Precedence for Documents
In the event of a conflict between this document and other documents specified herein, the
requirements of this document shall apply. In the event of a conflict between this document and
the contract, the contractual requirements shall take precedence over this document. In the event
of a conflict between this document and higher-level documents, the higher-level documents
shall take precedence over this document.

All documents used, applicable or reference, are to be the versions defined in the current version
of the SpaceDOC contract. Nothing in this document supersedes applicable laws and regulations
unless a specific exemption has been obtained.

3.0           MDCA OVERVIEW

3.1           Payload Description
The Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus is a mini-facility designed to support Principal
Investigators (PI) interested in studying various aspects of droplet combustion in a microgravity
environment. MDCA will be integrated into the Fluids and Combustion Facility’s (FCF)
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) onboard the International Space Station (ISS). Currently, the
Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) and the Flame Extinguishment Experiment 2 (FLEX-
2) have been selected for use in the MDCA.

3.2           MDCA Mission
The MDCA mission is to perform microgravity experiments to study fire suppression/flame
extinguishment investigations using the CIR. The MDCA will allow investigation using pure
liquid fuels and mixtures of liquid fuels at various chamber atmosphere pressures, compositions,
and oxygen concentrations. The microgravity environment allows for measurement and
observation of flame extinguishment processes that cannot be made in sustained gravity. The
modular design of the MDCA allows for flexibility in configuring for specific experiments and
easy maintainability of the hardware. This hardware will provide the apparatus for dispensing,
deploying and igniting fuel droplets. When new droplet experiments are proposed, the additional
experiment specific hardware will be provided. This requirements document reflects such a
case, including only the requirements of the FLEX-2 investigation.

3.3           FLEX-2 Requirements Flow
Figure 1 represents the requirements flow for all of the FLEX-2 requirements. The requirements
in the Science Requirements Document (SRD) are agreed upon by the FLEX-2 Principle
Investigators (PI’s), and this document serves as the top level source of those requirements
necessary to achieve the FLEX-2 science objectives. Derived requirements come from
engineering requirements and are set by the FLEX-2 Project Team. These two sets of
requirements are incorporated into this the FLEX-2 Engineering Requirements Document (FLX-
REQ-0001).

Safety requirements are contained in the updated FLEX-2 safety review hazard reports from the
Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP). The carrier requirements are found in the CIR/FLEX-2
Interface Control Document (FCF-ICD-CIR-MDCA).

3.4            MDCA Hardware Description
The FLEX-2 investigation will be using the existing MDCA hardware and software. MDCA
should be considered the platform on which the FLEX-2 experiments are carried out. The
MDCA hardware consists of three hardware domains: the Chamber Insert Assembly (CIA), the
Avionics Package, and MDCA Diagnostics. The CIA provides the mechanism for the
combustion event. The Avionics Package is the center of the control and power distribution for
the FLEX-2. The FLEX-2 hardware is discussed in detail below. If more detail is desired,
please refer to MDC-DOC-1364, MDCA Baseline Systems Description.

3.4.1          MDCA Chamber Insert Assembly
The MDCA Chamber Insert Assembly provides all the necessary hardware and interfaces to
perform science on one platform. Most experimental functions occur within the CIA structure
and many associated systems are found on the CIA. The CIA consists of the Internal Apparatus
(IA), which is the functional hardware and the Experiment Mounting Structure (EMS) upon
which the IA is structurally based. Other subsystems found on the CIA include the Droplet
Dispensing System, the Droplet Deployment System, the Fiber Support System, and the Ignition
System.

3.4.1.1        Experiment Mounting Structure
The EMS provides the main structure for the CIA and acts as the primary mechanical interface
with the CIR combustion chamber. It consists of two endplates, the support structure, and the
removable shrouds to protect the IA during crew activity.

3.4.1.2        Internal Apparatus
The IA provides the primary mounting platform for all experiment specific hardware and
functions such as droplet dispensing, deployment and ignition. The IA encompasses all motors
used in MDCA, as well as a cooling plate, radiometers, and some avionics hardware. The IA is
also available for future add-on hardware for different PIs.

3.4.1.2.1      Fuel Dispenser System
There are two separate fuel dispenser systems on the CIA. Each fuel dispenser system consists
of a motor housing and a replaceable reservoir. The motor housing is permanently fixed to the
IA and contains the motor, encoder, and lead screw assembly. The encoder verifies position of
the motor and allows ground operators to keep account of fuel usage. The replaceable reservoir
is composed of the syringe, the latching solenoid valve, the reservoir housing, and a transparent
Lexan cover. The replaceable reservoir assembly is located on top of the motor housing. The
syringe is covered in a Tygon sleeve and contained in aluminum housing. The syringe is
connected directly to a fuel isolation, latching, solenoid valve. The polytetraflouroethylene
(PTFE) fuel line tubing is attached to the valve with a removable fitting to disconnect the

deployment needles from the fuel system. Fuel is dispensed by moving the lead screw using a
stepper motor, which in turn pushes the plunger on the syringe.

3.4.1.2.2      Deployment System
The deployment system consists of two deployment needles made from .010-inch O.D. stainless
steel tubing supported by a ceramic sleeve. Each needle tip is flared to aid in the droplet
deployment. The needles are mounted to individual rotary servomotors with a specially designed
coupling that allows replacement of the needles and maintains the precise alignment of the
system. The motors rotate the needles to a pre-determined location where they are nearly tip-to-
tip. Metered fuel from the dispenser is routed via the PTFE tubing to one needle forming a
droplet of very precise volume. The deployment motors then actuate again, creating a slight gap
between the needles. This causes the droplet to center itself between the needle tips and
minimizes the contact area with the needles. Finally, the needles are rapidly accelerated apart,
deploying the droplet off the needle tips. The rapid acceleration leaves the droplet in place with
little or no residual motion.

3.4.1.2.3      Fiber Support System
The fiber mechanism consists of a 235 mm long, 79μm diameter silicon carbide fiber fastened
between two arms with epoxy to a tension of 15000 psi. There is a succession of small stainless
steel beads secured to the fiber at 12mm intervals. The use of the fiber mechanism allows fuel
droplets to be deployed onto, and thus tethered to, the beaded fiber at specific locations during
experimental burn and observation. The beads act to constrain the position of the droplets on the
fiber, which is especially necessary for the FLEX-2 droplet linear array experiments, where two
droplets are burned simultaneously. When used, the fiber is rotated 68o into the deployment area
using a rotary stepping gear motor. To deploy a linear array of droplets and to provide a clean
portion of the fiber for successive burns, linear translation of the fiber through the deployment
zone is achievable using a similar gear motor driving a pinion gear attached to a rack on the fiber
mechanism assembly. This translation can also be used to provide a low velocity flow over a
single burning droplet.

3.4.1.2.4      Ignition System
The ignition system uses the original MDCA configuration for single droplet ignition and for the
array experiments, modified dual droplet igniter tips are employed. The original MDCA ignition
system consists of two hot wire igniters opposed 180o, controlled by individual actuators. These
ignition wires are 4mm diameter loops of Kanthal A-1 wire, 30 AWG. These loops are mounted
into ceramic tubes and comprise the igniter tip assembly. This assembly has two pins that mate
with sockets on the igniter-mounting interface. This interface is fixed to the igniter motors,
which move the igniters into the deployment area linearly in precise steps and quickly retract the
igniters after ignition. The MDCA igniter tips are designed to be crew replaceable and for the
array experiments these will be replaced with the dual droplet igniter tips, which are based on the
original MDCA design and comply with all MDCA requirements.

3.4.1.2.5      Cooling Plate System
A cooling plate is provided to conductively cool the IA. The tubing is a stainless steel 3/8-inch
O.D. with .028-inch wall thickness. CIR compatible quick disconnect coupling fittings will
connect the cold plate to the EMS endplate. A flexible conductive lined Teflon hose with
stainless steel braiding will provide the coupling from the MDCA CIA to the CIR Interface
Resource Ring (IRR). Mating Preece connectors will be used for this interface with CIR’s IRR.
CIR’s color coding scheme will be maintained by MDCA for the inlet and outlet connectors.

The cooling system will circulate ISS cooling water flow controlled by CIR to satisfy FLEX-2
requirements. Prior to launch, the cooling system will be pre-filled to capacity with cooling
water. A gaseous nitrogen charged accumulator bottle installed inline will provide automatic
CIA protection from fluid over expansion in the system specifically during storage periods where
ambient temperatures may significantly change.

3.4.1.2.6      Radiometers
The Radiometers will provide relative measure of flame radiation and emissions through the
combustion event. The Radiometer Package consists of two Radiometers contained in a single
housing, mounted on the CIA, providing a direct view of the combustion event. The Broad-Band
Radiometer will measure total flame energy from combustion over a wavelength range covering
0.6 μm – 5.0 μm, while the Narrow-Band Radiometer will provide spectrally filtered
measurements for specific H20 emissions at 1.87 μm, using a narrow bandpass filter. Power to
the Radiometer Package is provided by MDCA Avionics.

3.4.2          MDCA Avionics
The Avionics Package provides power conditioning and power distribution, system control, data
acquisition, and operator interface for the MDCA. The Avionics Package will house the main
electronics for the MDCA hardware and will be mounted on the CIR Optics Bench.

3.4.2.1        Data and Control
A processor is responsible for automating the sequencing of operational events along with
acquiring, downlinking, and storing experiment data. Experiment control and sequencing will be
automated by the MDCA software, which is resident on the main processor. The main processor
communicates with the CIR Input/Output Processor (IOP). The interface to the CIR IOP is
necessary for transferring commands, downlinked data, and images and to receive the ISS video
and health and science (H&S) data.

3.4.2.2       Power Control and Distribution
MDCA receives its direct current, 28-Volt power from the CIR’s Electrical Power Control Unit
(EPCU) through the Avionics Package. In the Avionics Package, the power is conditioned by
filters and dc-dc converters for use by the processor, eight Axis Motor Controller, A/D and
Signal Conditioning Boards, and CIA interface board.

3.4.3         MDCA Diagnostics
MDCA Diagnostics provide acquisition and storage of all optical information concerning droplet
deployment and combustion.

3.4.3.1       Color Camera Package
The MDCA Color Camera Package will provide an overhead view of the combustion event. The
Color Camera Package consists of a Sony FCB-EX470L CCD camera, which includes a built-in
Zoom Lens with RS-232 controllable zoom and focus functions. The camera is completely
enclosed in a housing container and mounted to the CIA upper structure, internal to the chamber.
An aluminum broadband coated turning mirror is used to fold the view from the experiment to
the color camera. The Color Camera Package analog video output is converted to twisted pair,
via the Color Camera Interface Package, which then routes the output to the CIR Image
Processing and Storage Unit (IPSU-A) for viewing and storage. Power to the Color Camera
Package is supplied by MDCA Avionics.

3.4.3.2       White Light Illumination
The White Light Illumination Package supports the Color Camera Package prior to and
following the experiment event, to provide direct overhead lighting of the droplet deployment
area during dispensing, deployment and ignition for troubleshooting purposes. The White Light
Illumination is powered off upon droplet ignition, as the experiment provides its own light. The
package consists of two clusters of nine White Light LEDs mounted on the CIA upper structure.
Power to the White Light Illumination is supplied by MDCA Avionics.

3.5             Interfaces

3.5.1           External Interfaces

3.5.1.1         Launch Configuration Interfaces
FLEX-2 provided hardware is non-operational for launch. FLEX-2 hardware will be stowed in
standard containers provided by FLEX-2 and will only have physical and structural interfaces
with the containers.

3.5.1.2         On-Orbit External Interfaces
FLEX-2 has no direct external interfaces on-orbit. All interfaces with the FCF, US LAB, ISS
and the ground are indirectly through CIR.

3.5.2           Internal Interfaces
The internal interfaces between MDCA and CIR are listed below and the requirements for these
interfaces will be defined in FCF-ICD-CIR-MDCA, Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus
Interface Control Document.

•     Structural/Mechanical and Stowage
•     Electrical Power
•     Command and Data Handling
•     Payload and Diagnostics
•     Thermal Control
•     Exhaust Vent
•     FOMA Gas Delivery
•     Environmental

4.0            REQUIREMENTS
This section details all science and derived engineering requirements that have been levied upon
FLEX-2. Verifications for these requirements are documented in the FLEX-2 SEVP (FLX-PLN-
0002).

4.1            Science Requirements
This section is a flowdown of the science requirements from the FLEX-2 SRD dated December
6, 2009. Upon being signed, this FLEX-2 ERD becomes the formal FLEX-2 project requirement
document.

4.1.1          Experimental Fuels - Alcohol
FLEX-2 shall require the use of ethanol.

4.1.2          Experimental Fuels – Hydrocarbon
FLEX-2 shall require the use of decane.

4.1.3          Experimental Fuels – Alcohol Mixture
FLEX-2 shall require the use of a propanol/glycerol mixture.

4.1.4          Experimental Fuels – Hydrocarbon Mixture 1
FLEX-2 shall require the use of a heptane/hexadecane mixture.

4.1.5          Experimental Fuels – Hydrocarbon Mixture 2
FLEX-2 shall require the use of a heptane/octane mixture.

4.1.6          Experimental Fuels – Other Mixture
FLEX-2 shall require the use of a decane/propylbenzene mixture.

4.1.7          Fuel Purity
FLEX-2 shall use fuels of research grade with purity greater than 99.5% by volume.

4.1.8          Fuel Quality
FLEX-2 fuels shall be anhydrous prior to loading into fuel reservoirs.

4.1.9          Fuel Degassing
FLEX-2 pure fuels shall be degassed prior to loading into fuel reservoirs.

4.1.10         Fuel Quality Assurance
Certification of test samples shall be provided prior to flight.

4.1.11         Fuel Temperature
The fuel temperature at the start of each test shall be in the range of 18 ºC – 27 ºC.

4.1.12         Droplet Size Tolerance
FLEX-2 shall dispense droplets with diameters of 1.5 – 5 mm with a tolerance ± 0.25 mm.

4.1.13         Droplet Size Reproducibility
FLEX-2 shall dispense droplets with diameters of 1.5 – 5 mm with a reproducibility of ± 5%.

4.1.14         Fiber Size
FLEX-2 shall provide a support fiber with a diameter < 100 µm.

4.1.15         Fiber Material Thermal Diffusivity
FLEX-2 shall provide a fiber material with a thermal diffusivity no greater than 2.3 cm2/s.

4.1.16         Fiber Material Emissivity
FLEX-2 shall provide a fiber material with an emissivity comparable to that of 80 micron.
diameter Silicon Carbide.

4.1.17         Droplet Anchoring Capability
FLEX-2 shall provide a support fiber capable of anchoring a fuel droplet at a fixed location by
use of bead structures.

4.1.18         Droplet Arrays
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to create droplet arrays in a binary linear configuration with
bead spacing of 12mm and 24mm.

4.1.19         Bead Material
FLEX-2 shall ensure that the beads are made of an impervious material.

4.1.20         Bead Shape
FLEX-2 shall ensure that the beads are of a shape that is as close to spherical as possible.

4.1.21         Bead Size
FLEX-2 shall ensure that the beads have a diameter that is as small as possible, but of sufficient
size as to allow consistent droplet deployment and positioning for the full range of initial droplet
diameters.

4.1.22         Bead Surface
FLEX-2 shall ensure that the surface of the beads and the fiber interface contain no pores or
areas where gas can be trapped.

4.1.23         Bead Spacing
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to create droplet arrays in a binary linear configuration with
a bead spacing of 12mm.

4.1.24         Ignite in Flow
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to ignite a droplet in a quiescent atmosphere and with gas
flowing past.

4.1.25         Igniter Material
FLEX-2 shall provide hot wire igniters as the droplet ignition source.

4.1.26         Igniter on Time
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to power on the igniters for between 1 to 5 second durations.

4.1.27         Ignition Timing
FLEX-2 shall wait 10 seconds after deployment of a droplet before initiating the ignition
sequence to allow for droplet deployment induced oscillations to damp adequately.

4.1.28         Ignition Disturbance
FLEX-2 shall provide the command controllable ability to apply the minimum necessary energy
input to the droplet during ignition.

4.1.29         Igniter Position Control
FLEX-2 shall provide capability to reposition the igniter tip between tests to 1 – 5 initial droplet
diameters from the droplet surface, ± 0.5 mm.

4.1.30         Igniter Retraction
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to retract the igniter tips from the field of view of the droplet
view diagnostic after ignition of the droplet.

4.1.31         Igniter Control
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to change the igniter position, power, and duration of
operation by command.

4.1.32         Hardware Exclusion
FLEX-2 shall provide for removal of all objects (except the fiber) inside the spherical boundary
of a radius of 10 initial droplet diameters from the deployment site after ignition during all tests.

4.1.33         Non-Quiescent Test Point Timing
When running a non-quiescent test point, the translation of the support fiber shall begin at the
same time as igniter retraction.

4.1.34         Chamber Atmosphere Pressure
FLEX-2 shall provide ambient pressure ranges from 0.5 – 3 atm, with a tolerance of ± 0.05 atm.

4.1.35         Chamber Atmosphere Pressure Rise
FLEX-2 shall maintain the chamber pressure throughout any given test point to within ± 10% of
the initial chamber pressure.

4.1.36         Oxygen Mole Fractions
FLEX-2 shall provide oxygen mole fractions ranging from 0.1 to 0.4 with a tolerance on the
initial charge of ± 0.005 for O2.

4.1.37         Chamber Atmosphere Temperature
FLEX-2 shall provide ambient temperature within the range of 18 – 27 °C.

4.1.38         Atmospheric Mixing
FLEX-2 shall provide well-mixed chamber gasses before ignition.

4.1.39         Atmospheric Quiescence
FLEX-2 shall provide quiescent gasses prior to ignition.

4.1.40         Atmospheric Humidity
Atmosphere shall have a Relative Humidity of < 10% for all tests.

4.1.41         Chamber Atmosphere Test Set 1
FLEX-2 shall provide gas mixtures of O2/N2.

4.1.42         Chamber Atmosphere Test Set 2
FLEX-2 shall provide gas mixtures of O2/He.

4.1.43         Flow Field Production
FLEX-2 shall provide relative motion between the drop and the ambient gas by translating the
fiber.

4.1.44         Flow Field Velocity Ranges
FLEX-2 shall provide flow velocity ranges from 0.1 to 5cm/s with an accuracy of ±1%.

4.1.45         Flow Field Control
FLEX-2 shall provide for control of the acceleration and deceleration of the flow field.

4.1.46         Test Point Initiation
FLEX-2 shall wait at least two (2) minutes after a chamber atmospheric fill before beginning a
test point to ensure the gas, temperature and pressure to stabilize.

4.1.47         Display of Diagnostic Views
FLEX-2 shall provide the capability to downlink the color camera view in near real time.

4.1.48         Downlink of Chamber Temperature Data
FLEX-2 shall provide near real time downlink of the chamber temperature data.

The test atmosphere prior to each test point shall have fuel vapor mole fraction of < 0.005.

The test atmosphere prior to each test shall consist of < 0.02 mole fraction (for each product

FLEX-2 shall ensure acceleration levels are < 1 x 10-4 m/s2 on three (3) axes.

4.1.53         Microgravity Measurement
FLEX-2 shall provide capability to measure acceleration near the CIR with an accuracy of 1 x
10-6 m/s2. Frequency range shall be 0.01 – 125 Hz. Sampling rate shall be 1 – 5 times the
frequency.

and post-extinction.

coplanar with the droplet.

view.

4.1.57         Droplet Imaging Spatial Resolution
FLEX-2 shall provide spatial resolution of 30 µm over the entire FOV for the droplet view.

4.1.58         Droplet Imaging Temporal Resolution
FLEX-2 shall provide a nominal minimum framing rate of 30 fps for the droplet view.

4.1.69        Color Imaging Orientation
FLEX-2 shall ensure the MDCA color camera provides a full view of the droplet and flame with
the focal plane parallel to the fiber providing viewing of the droplet dispensing and deployment
sequence.

4.1.70        Color Imaging FOV
FLEX-2 shall provide a FOV ≥ 5.0 cm diameter, positioned so the entire flame is imaged for the
MDCA color camera.

4.1.71        Color Imaging Spatial Resolution
FLEX-2 shall provide a spatial resolution of 100μm for the MDCA color camera.

4.1.72        Color Imaging Temporal Resolution
FLEX-2 shall provide framing rate of 30 fps for the MDCA color camera.

4.1.73        Color Imaging DOF
FLEX-2 shall provide a DOF of no less than 5.0 mm for the MDCA color camera.

4.1.74        Color Imaging Zoom
FLEX-2 shall provide a zoom capability with the MDCA color camera, upon request of the PI, in
order to adjust the FOV.

4.1.75        Narrow Band Radiative Emission
FLEX-2 shall provide a narrow band radiometer to measure radiant emissions in the luminous
and non-luminous flames at a wavelength in the H2O band centered at 1.87 µm.

4.1.76        Narrow and Broad Band Radiative Emission Sampling Rate
FLEX-2 shall provide a narrowband and broadband radiometer sampling rate of 30 Hz.

4.1.77        Narrow Band and Broad Band Radiative Emission Placement
FLEX-2 shall place the narrowband and broadband radiometer at least 15 cm from the droplet.

4.1.78        Narrow Band and Broad Band Radiometer Isolation
FLEX-2 shall shield the narrowband and broadband radiometers from igniter wire radiation, both
reflected and direct.

4.1.79         Narrow Band and Broad Band Radiative Emission Accuracy
The FLEX-2 narrow band and broad band radiative emission accuracy shall be 5% of full scale
incident radiation.

4.1.80         Narrow Band and Broad Band Radiative Emission Response Time
The FLEX-2 narrow band and broad band radiative emission shall have a response time constant
of less than 40 ms.

4.1.81         Narrow Band and Broad Band Radiative Emission FOV
FLEX-2 shall provide a narrowband and broadband radiometer FOV of 65 mm in diameter,
centered about the deployment site.

4.1.82         Broad Band Radiative Emission
FLEX-2 shall employ a broad band radiometer to measure radiant emissions in the luminous and
non-luminous flames in the wavelength range of 0.6-5.0 µm.

4.1.83         Soot Volume Fraction Imaging Orientation
FLEX-2 shall provide a full view of the droplet and flame with a preferred orientation such that
the focal plane is parallel to the fiber and coplanar with the droplet.

4.1.84         Soot Volume Fraction Backlight
FLEX-2 shall provide a collimated backlit soot volume fraction diagnostic with the backlight at a
wavelength of 660 nm and a Full Width Half Maximum of 5 nm.

4.1.85         Soot Volume Fraction Temporal Resolution
FLEX-2 shall provide a soot volume fraction diagnostic with a framing rate of ≥ 15 fps.

4.1.86         Soot Volume Fraction Spatial Resolution
FLEX-2 shall provide a soot volume fraction diagnostic with a resolution of 50 μm over the
entire FOV.

4.1.87         Soot Volume Fraction Field of View
FLEX-2 shall provide a soot volume fraction diagnostic with a full view of the droplet and
flame, having a FOV ≥ 5.0 cm centered on the droplet deployment site.

4.1.97           Temperature Measurement Accuracy
FLEX-2 shall provide ambient temperature measurement accuracy to within ±0.5 C in the range
of 18-27º C.

4.1.98           Synchronization of Measurements
FLEX-2 shall reference time measurements to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) and have all data

4.2              Derived Requirements
This section specifies the additional derived requirements needed to support the training, testing,
operations, design, and development of the FLEX-2 project within the MDCA and CIR carriers.

4.2.1            Fuel Dispenser System
The following requirements refer specifically to the MDCA/FLEX-2 fuel dispenser system.

4.2.1.1          Fuel Mixture Ratio Accuracy
FLEX-2 shall develop a procedure to ensure that accurate fuel mixtures are loaded into the fuel
reservoirs. Mixture ratios shall be accurate to within ±0.5%.

4.2.1.2          Fuel Material Compatibility
The materials exposed to the fuels within the dispensing system shall be compatible with FLEX-
2 identified fuels as follows:

1.   Ethanol
      2.   Decane
      3.   Heptane
      4.   Hexadecane
      5.   Octane
      6.   Propylbenzene
      7.   Glycerol
      8.   Propanol

4.2.1.3          Purity Degradation
Purity degradation is in direct correlation to the fuels’ exposure to outside environments. Fuel
purity degradation shall be ensured by sealing the fuel reservoir assembly to a maximum leak
rate of 1 x 10-6 scc/sec of gaseous helium.

4.2.2            Atmospheric Conditions
The following requirements refer specifically to FLEX-2 chamber atmospheric conditions.

The following requirements refer specifically to the hardware components found on the MDCA
Internal Apparatus.

4.2.3.1        Oxygen Compatibility
All components developed for FLEX-2 located in the CIR chamber shall be compatible with

4.2.3.2        Igniter Compatibility
FLEX-2 shall provide igniter tips that comply with the existing MDCA igniter drive circuitry.

resistance of 1 Ω ± 0.250Ω at 20°C.

4.2.3.4        Fiber Alignment with Needles
The fiber shall be oriented orthogonal to the needle line of action within ± 5 degrees. This value
shall be maintained for all replaceable units (when a component is replaced, it shall have the
same alignment).
